prompt: Each practice comes from a firm that uses algorithms in marketing or finance. Identify which form of visibility it provides.

cases.text: An online retailer adds a line to its chat window: 'You are talking to an automated assistant.'
cases.explanation: Disclosing that an automated system is in use is institutional openness about the process; it says nothing about how the model computes.

cases.text: An insurer prices renters' policies with a five-variable scorecard; an analyst can read each variable's points straight off the table.
cases.explanation: The model's own structure is simple enough to trace how inputs combine into the price, so no secondary procedure is needed.

cases.text: After a neural network ranks loyalty-programme members, the analytics team fits a small decision tree to its outputs to summarize what it seems to do.
cases.explanation: A surrogate model fitted after the fact approximates the black box; it is not the model that made the ranking.

cases.text: A bank publishes the auditing standard its credit models must pass and the provenance of the data they were trained on.
cases.explanation: Publishing governance and auditing standards and documenting data provenance are forms of process transparency.

cases.text: A lender runs an attribution procedure on its gradient-boosted model to list which features pushed one applicant's score down.
cases.explanation: The attribution is a secondary mathematical procedure that summarizes the black box's output after the fact.

prompt: Following the governance reasoning on the slide, sort each task by the kind of model it should use.

cards.text: Approving or declining mortgage applications from income, debt, and repayment history.
cards.explanation: High-stakes consumer credit on structured tabular features: an interpretable model with monotonicity constraints avoids hidden edge-case failures.

cards.text: Scoring hospital patients' readmission risk from lab values and age to decide who gets follow-up care.
cards.explanation: Medical risk scoring on tabular data carries severe human consequences, so exact interpretability is preferred.

cards.text: Recognising which products appear in shoppers' uploaded photos.
cards.explanation: Raw images are unstructured data, where black-box architectures provide genuine performance advantages.

cards.text: Ordering songs in a music app's 'Up next' list, after a test shows the complex model lifts listening time.
cards.explanation: A lower-stakes ranking task where the accuracy gain has been verified to outweigh the loss of exact interpretability.

cards.text: Recommending pretrial release from a defendant's age, prior offences, and missed court dates.
cards.explanation: Criminal justice decisions on structured features are high-stakes; an approximate post-hoc explanation could hide critical failures.

cards.text: Summarising the topics of thousands of free-text customer service transcripts for a weekly report.
cards.explanation: Free text is unstructured language data, the domain where black-box models are reserved for use.

prompt: Each audit note describes a problem with a post-hoc attribution. Identify the limitation at work.

cases.text: Rerunning LIME for the same insurance customer with a different random seed moves 'vehicle age' from the top driver to fourth place.
cases.explanation: A small change in the random seed changed the ranking of drivers for the same customer.

cases.text: A manager reads a high SHAP value for 'postal code' and concludes that moving house would lower a customer's default risk.
cases.explanation: The attribution reflects predictive association inside the model, not a causal mechanism in the world.

cases.text: A vendor's model routes inputs that look like synthetic perturbations to a fair sub-model and real applicant profiles to a biased one.
cases.explanation: Wrapping a discriminatory model in an out-of-distribution detector fools LIME and SHAP while it keeps discriminating on real customers.

cases.text: To score 'job tenure', the procedure pairs a 25-year tenure with an applicant whose income and age match a first-year graduate.
cases.explanation: Varying one of two correlated features on its own creates an off-manifold, unrealistic customer profile.

cases.text: Switching the SHAP background sample from last year's customers to this year's changes which feature an auditor reports as the main driver.
cases.explanation: The background reference distribution is one of the settings whose small changes can reorder the top drivers.

prompt: A rejected loan applicant receives each of these suggested changes. Sort them by whether they offer actionable recourse.

cards.text: Pay down your card balance so that utilization falls below 30 percent.
cards.explanation: Utilization is a mutable feature the applicant can change through their own actions.
Age is immutable; it can explain a score but offers zero recourse.

cards.text: Have been born in a different country.
cards.explanation: Birthplace is immutable and may also be a protected attribute.

cards.text: Report three fewer years of work experience.
cards.explanation: Work experience can only grow; asking it to decrease is a directionally infeasible change.

cards.text: Not have missed a car payment five years ago.
cards.explanation: Past payment history is conditionally immutable: it cannot be changed now.

cards.text: Add 2,000 dollars to your savings account over the next six months.
cards.explanation: Savings is mutable and moves in a feasible direction (up).

cards.text: Lower your highest completed degree from a master's to a bachelor's.
cards.explanation: Educational attainment only moves upward, so a decrease is not a feasible direction.

question_text: An auditor gives a language model twenty laptop comparisons in which the cheaper laptop is always listed first. The model picks the first-listed laptop 90 percent of the time, and each chain-of-thought explains the pick with battery life and build quality, never with list order. What best describes these explanations?
hint: Separate how convincing the explanation reads from whether it names what actually drove the choice.
correct_answer_citation: Week 05 · Plausibility Versus Faithfulness in LLM Explanations

options.option_text: Faithful but implausible: the reasons are correct but read poorly.
options.option_explanation: The reasons read well, and they leave out the actual driver, so they are neither implausible nor faithful.

options.option_text: Both plausible and faithful, because battery life and build quality are sensible criteria.
options.option_explanation: Sensible-sounding criteria make an explanation plausible; faithfulness requires naming the true causal factor, list order.

options.option_text: Plausible but unfaithful: the traces read as convincing while omitting the covert ordering cue that drove the choice.
options.option_explanation: Correct. This matches Turpin and colleagues' finding: a covert cue biases the choice while the trace rationalizes it with neutral-sounding criteria.

options.option_text: Faithful, because the trace is a readout of the network's attention activations.
options.option_explanation: A reasoning trace is a sequence of predicted tokens conditioned on the prompt, not a diagnostic readout of weights or activations.

prompt: Each finding pairs a controlled choice experiment with coded reasoning traces. Sort it by what the pairing shows.

cards.text: Adding an eco-label raises an agent's choice of a detergent by 20 points, and coded traces mention the label in most labelled sessions.
cards.explanation: The manipulation shifts both the coded trace and the choice, so the trace supports the behavioral mechanism.

cards.text: Swapping a brand name from a domestic to a foreign one lowers choice of an identical product by 15 points, yet no trace ever mentions the brand's origin.
cards.explanation: The choice moves with the manipulated factor while the trace never names it: the divergence exposes hidden bias.

cards.text: Telling an agent the order is urgent raises its choice of next-day delivery, and coded traces state delivery speed as the goal more often.
cards.explanation: Stated goal and choice move together under the manipulation, giving convergent process-tracing evidence.

cards.text: Placing a hotel in the first slot raises its selection by 12 points across conditions, while every trace credits its reviews and location.
cards.explanation: Position drives the choice but the trace rationalizes it with neutral-sounding criteria.

cards.text: A sponsorship label lowers choice of a listing, and coded traces show more stated skepticism toward that listing in the same condition.
cards.explanation: Both the coded skepticism and the choice probability shift with the label, as in audits of sponsorship disclosure.

prompt: Match each person with the explanation that serves the decision they must make.

pairs.term: A data scientist investigating why a churn model fails on new customers
pairs.match: Global feature attributions and ICE curves
pairs.explanation: Engineers and internal auditors debug spurious correlations with global attributions and ICE curves.

pairs.term: A chief product officer deciding whether to launch a pricing model
pairs.match: A model card and an accuracy-fairness trade-off frontier
pairs.explanation: Executives authorize deployment and allocate risk from model cards and trade-off frontiers.

pairs.term: A conformity assessor reviewing a high-risk hiring system
pairs.match: A standardized audit trail with disparate-impact ratios
pairs.explanation: Regulators need audit trails, disparate-impact ratios, and provenance sheets as evidence of compliance.

pairs.term: A renter whose apartment application was declined by an automated screen
pairs.match: A plain-language reason and a feasible step that would change the outcome
pairs.explanation: Affected consumers need notice, plain-language reasons, and actionable counterfactual recourse.
